title: When money markets stop trading: Carney on credit supply and the need for further easing
summary: In London on 19 November 2008, Governor Mark Carney put two seemingly inconsistent observations together. Canadian banks continued lending to firms and households, yet the Bank of Canada would probably need to provide more monetary stimulus. A bank can still extend a loan while its export customers lose orders, commodity income falls and the spread on that loan rises. The first part of his address asks how to keep financing available in a crisis. The closing Canadian outlook asks what interest-rate setting will bring inflation back to target. Each question implies a different test of policy transmission (opening remarks and “The Canadian Perspective”).

Carney’s diagnosis begins with the reversal from financing through securities markets to relying on bank balance sheets. When securities cease trading, transferring intermediation back to banks requires capital precisely when it is hardest to raise. Funds expecting redemptions sell foreign assets, while banks favour borrowers they know close to home. Capital can therefore flow away from an emerging economy even when its domestic institutions have done little to change their own behaviour. A dataset of completed transactions can miss the worst part of the contraction. The spread on the last commercial-paper issue tells little about a borrower that can no longer issue at any price (PDF, pp. 2–4).

He links this breakdown to decisions made during the preceding period of low volatility. Credit ratings had displaced investors’ own scrutiny of the underlying assets. Originators could pass loans on, and internal funding charges could underprice a trading desk’s use of the bank’s balance sheet. Rising collateral margins then forced borrowers to raise cash as asset values fell. In this account, an increase in the supply of central-bank funds alone cannot resolve uncertainty about a counterparty’s solvency or restore the information investors need to price an opaque security. Carney supported system-wide prudential oversight alongside inflation targeting. He regarded the policy rate as a poor instrument for targeting asset prices (PDF, pp. 2–4).

His two routes back to functioning markets put the public intervention at different points in the chain. Under the G7 strategy, capital and funding support for core institutions should allow banks to resume market-making and private lending. Its success depends on those institutions passing funding on. Carney also discussed a central bank standing ready to transact with a wider set of market participants when private intermediaries retreat. Money funds’ withdrawal from non-government securities could deprive issuers of buyers even if banks themselves had liquidity. He presented direct market-making as an option for policy makers. The speech did not establish a new Canadian facility or report transactions under one (PDF, pp. 4–5).

Carney used the balance sheets of major Canadian banks to explain why he expected the first route to work in Canada. Their consolidated assets averaged 18 times capital against a regulatory ceiling of 20. His comparators were above 25 for US investment banks, in the thirties for European banks and above 40 at some large international banks. Only about one fifth of Canadian mortgages had been securitized. He associated retained exposure with underwriting discipline and pointed to insurance on high loan-to-value mortgages and the sovereign guarantee on Canada Mortgage Bonds. These comparisons identify differences in institutions and incentives. The ratios alone cannot attribute a lending outcome to leverage when guarantees, loan books and business models also differ (PDF, pp. 5–6).

The near-term tension concerned how quickly to rebuild capital. A bank facing an immediate increase in its required ratio can meet it by reducing assets. If many banks do so during a downturn, weaker activity can increase loan losses, eroding capital again. Carney argued for allowing ratios to decline through the downturn and staggering necessary increases. For market infrastructure, he discussed clearing credit derivatives centrally, the costs of margining and the possibility of steadier collateral requirements through the cycle. A historical study would need to record which items were proposals and identify a separate implementation date for any subsequent change (PDF, pp. 4–6).

Carney’s Canadian policy signal is explicit near the end. Wider credit spreads, falling commodity prices, weaker terms of trade and US housing and auto weakness had moved risks to the downside relative to the October Monetary Policy Report. Domestic demand and a weaker Canadian dollar provided offsets. The Bank had already halved official interest rates over the preceding year and he saw further stimulus as likely. That statement gives a direction conditional on the outlook, without specifying the size or date of a cut. Its surprise to investors requires prices or forecasts from before the remarks. A fall in a corporate yield after the speech would itself leave two open possibilities: a lower expected overnight-rate path or a narrowing spread over that path (PDF, p. 6).

questions.question: Did access to market finance improve for issuers that had lost it altogether?
questions.detail: Build a weekly panel of borrowers that issued commercial paper before stress intensified, keeping an issuer in the sample when it has no new issue. Compare new volumes, rollover shares, maturities and borrowing costs across issuers with and without bank credit lines. Match borrowers on pre-crisis quality and refinancing needs. A lower average spread among the survivors alongside more zero-issuance weeks would undermine the inference that the market had reopened.

questions.question: How far did Canadian banks transmit public term funding to private borrowers?
questions.detail: Match the timing of announced operations and settlement to changes in term-funding spreads, credit-line drawdowns and new bank lending. Separate previously committed lending from newly approved credit, and compare banks with different pre-crisis funding reliance. Emergency use is likely highest at the most stressed institutions. A simple correlation between take-up and subsequent lending would mix that initial weakness with the effect of the intervention.

questions.question: What did markets learn about the overnight rate from Carney’s outlook?
questions.detail: Recover the public release time in London and the contemporaneous Canadian trading hours. Measure Canadian overnight-indexed swaps around the release alongside US rates, commodity prices and Canadian credit spreads. Check for overlapping crisis announcements before treating any short-window change as informative. A move concentrated in corporate funding spreads would tell a different story from a repricing of the next few policy meetings, even if both made finance cheaper.
